newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia to stick to rouble policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia to stick to rouble policy.

text.p: The Russian Central Bank will maintain its policy of a gentle rouble decline against the dollar next year, a senior bank official said on Monday.

Announcing another big rise in currency reserves, First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko told a news conference the Central Bank was pressing ahead with plans to make the rouble a reserve currency for other ex-Soviet republics and to encourage the use of the rouble rather than the dollar within Russia.
"We are not planning a change in hard currency policy next year," Aleksashenko said. "It will be a gradual depreciation of the rouble at a rate a bit lower than the inflation rate."
Monthly inflation in the first quarter of this year averaged 1.5 percent, while the depreciation of the rouble was less than one percent.
Aleksashenko said the bank had not yet decided whether to stick to the current system of currency bands, known as a sloping corridor, or use another method of currency control.

The rouble has been relatively steady since the Central Bank took the rouble/dollar rate under control two years ago by introducing a currency corridor. Under the policy the bank sets upper and lower rates for rouble fluctuation for a certain period, and announces daily buy/sell rates within the band.
The 1997 corridor envisages a rouble range of 5,750-6,350 to the dollar by the end of the year, against 5,500-6,100 at the start of the year. On Monday the rouble traded at 5,764/5,765.
The rouble has never strayed beyond the corridor, as the Central Bank intervenes on the market by buying or selling dollars from currency reserves if the danger appears.

Aleksashenko said gross reserves were currently around $19 billion. Net international reserves, which exclude loans from the International Monetary Fund and other short-term loans, had risen to 31 trillion roubles ($5.6 billion) on June 1 from 23.5 trillion on May 1.
The rise is due to Central Bank's dollar purchases on the currency market and Aleksashenko said the Bank was not yet sated with dollars.

Businesses profit from the policy as they can predict the rouble/dollar rates for months ahead. But banks have lost one source of profits as scope for speculating in the currency market has been severely limited.

The stability of the rouble has led the central bank of Belarus to place some of its reserves in Russian roubles. Aleksahsenko said the National Bank of Belarus had bought about 100 billion roubles of Russian Treasury bills.
"We think the terms offered by the Central Bank of Russia for placing hard currency reserves of neighbouring countries in roubles are more attractive than holding them in dollars," Aleksashenko said.

In another move to bolster the use of the rouble in Russia, the Central Bank will require roubles rather than dollars or other currencies be used from October 1 when paying with credit cards. The rouble is already the sole legal tender for cash payments.

The government hopes individuals will gradually use roubles rather than dollars as inflation falls and the rouble rate is kept steady. According to the Central Bank estimates individuals hold about $20 billion in cash.
Aleksashenko said recent Central Bank research showed most dollars bought at exchange points were purchased by people engaged in illegal foreign trade.

Aleksashenko said the Central Bank was not yet ready to let the rouble/dollar rate float freely for fear of a sharp fall in the dollar rate which would hurt exporters and households, who keep their savings in dollars.
